content: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a group of genetic disorders that affect hemoglobin, leading to the production of abnormally shaped red blood cells, often described as sickleor crescent-shaped. This condition is characterized by chronic anemia, increased vulnerability to infections, and recurrent episodes of pain. SCD is inherited when an individual receives abnormal hemoglobin genes from both parents, resulting in various forms of the disease. Due to the increased production of red blood cells (erythropoiesis) in individuals with SCD, it is hypothesized that they are at a higher risk of folate deficiency. Consequently, children and adults with SCD, particularly those with sickle cell anemia, are often prescribed 1 mg of folic acid daily to replenish folate stores and potentially alleviate anemia-related symptoms. Evaluating the role of folate supplementation in managing SCD is therefore of clinical importance. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and potential adverse effects of folate supplementation, whether derived from natural dietary sources, fortified foods, or additional supplements such as tablets, in individuals with SCD. A comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group’s Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, which includes references from electronic databases, hand-searched journals, and conference proceedings. Additional searches were performed in electronic databases and clinical trial registries. The last search of the trials register was conducted on November 17, 2017. The review included randomized, placebo-controlled trials of folate supplementation in individuals with SCD. Four authors independently assessed the eligibility and risk of bias of the included trials, extracted data, and analyzed the findings using standard Cochrane methodologies. The quality of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Only one trial, conducted in 1983, met the inclusion criteria. This was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, quasi-randomized trial investigating the effects of folic acid supplementation in children with homozygous sickle cell (SS) disease. A total of 117 children aged six months to four years participated in the study, which lasted one year. Data analysis was restricted to 115 children. Serum folate levels were measured at six and 12 months in 80 of the 115 participants (70%). The results showed significant differences in serum folate levels between the folic acid and placebo groups. In the folic acid group, 33 of 41 participants (81%) had serum folate levels above 18 µg/L, compared to only six of 39 participants (15%) in the placebo group. Additionally, no participants in the folic acid group had serum folate levels below 5 µg/L, whereas 15 of 39 participants (39%) in the placebo group had levels below this threshold. However, the quality of this evidence was rated as low. Hematological indices, including total hemoglobin concentrations, were measured in 100 of the 115 participants (87%) at baseline and after one year. After adjusting for sex and age, no significant differences in hemoglobin concentrations were observed between the folic acid and placebo groups at either time point. The quality of this evidence was also rated as low. It is important to note that raw data for these outcomes were not available for analysis. Clinical events, including minor infections, major infections, dactylitis, acute splenic sequestration, and pain episodes, were analyzed in all 115 participants, and raw data were available for these outcomes. No statistically significant differences were observed between the folic acid and placebo groups for any of these events. However, the trial was not adequately powered to detect such differences. The risk ratios (RR) for these outcomes were as follows: minor infections (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.15), major infections (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.66), dactylitis (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.27), acute splenic sequestration (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.57), and pain episodes (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.92). All evidence for these outcomes was of low quality. However, a higher proportion of repeat dactylitis episodes was reported in the placebo group, with two or more attacks occurring in 10 of 56 participants compared to two of 59 participants in the folic acid group (P < 0.05). Growth parameters, including height-for-age, weight-for-age, height, and growth velocity, were assessed in 103 of the 115 participants (90%). No significant differences in growth were reported between the folic acid and placebo groups. Raw data for these outcomes were not available. The trial was assessed to have a high risk of bias in terms of random sequence generation and incomplete outcome data. There was an unclear risk of bias regarding allocation concealment, outcome assessment, and selective reporting. However, the risk of bias related to blinding of participants and personnel was low. Overall, the quality of the evidence was rated as low. No other eligible trials were identified for comparisons such as folate supplementation (fortified foods or tablets) versus placebo, folate supplementation (naturally occurring in diet) versus placebo, or fortified/physical supplementation versus naturally occurring dietary folate. In conclusion, the review included one double-blind, placebo-controlled trial on folic acid supplementation in children with SCD. The evidence from this trial was mixed and of low quality. While folic acid supplementation appeared to increase serum folate levels, its effects on anemia and related symptoms remain unclear. No trials involving adults were identified. Future trials should aim to assess clinical outcomes such as folate and hemoglobin concentrations, as well as the potential benefits and adverse effects of folate supplementation. These trials should include participants of all ages and sexes, recruit larger sample sizes, and have longer durations with extended follow-up periods. However, it is unlikely that further trials on this intervention will be conducted, and as a result, this review will no longer be updated.
